extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of aesthetics (writers, poets, architects), general readers interested in the theory of the sublime and the beautiful
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the author's criteria for producing and recognising the sublime and the beautiful in art and description, including sensory causes (sound, smell, pain) and arguments rejecting proportion/utility as explanations of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid light and riant ornament when aiming for the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: When a melancholy kind of greatness (the highest form of sublimity) is intended, bright, cheerful, or sparkling ornamentation (gilding, mosaics, painting, statues, anything 'light and riant') should be avoided because such features 'effectually deaden the whole taste of the sublime.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this rule primarily where a uniform degree of the most striking sublimity is to be produced in every particular; in other buildings where grandeur must be studied, draw sublimity from other sources but strictly avoid anything light, gay, or cheerful that would undermine the sublime effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive loudness as a source of the sublime (sound and loudness)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Excessive loudness alone is sufficient to overpower the soul, to suspend its action, and to fill it with terror." Loud natural or artificial noises (vast cataracts, raging storms, thunder, artillery, shouting multitudes) awaken a great and awful sensation in the mind even without musical nicety or artifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for sublime effect, foreground overwhelming, powerful sounds; the sheer strength and scale of sound can create amazement and confound the imagination. Familiarity or musical refinement are not necessary; the magnitude of the sound itself is effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suddenness (abrupt beginnings or cessations) produces the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: "A sudden beginning, or sudden cessation of sound of any considerable force, has the same power." Suddenness rouses attention, produces a perception of danger, and drives the faculties forward on guard; smooth transitions remove terror and so cannot produce greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use abrupt onsets or sudden stops in sights or sounds to startle and produce sublime effect. Repetition of a single strong short sound at intervals (a clock striking in the night, a drum beat with pauses, successive distant cannon) intensifies the effect. Avoid making transitions from one extreme to the other easy or gradual if the goal is terror/sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermitting, low, tremulous sounds create sublime by uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: "A low, tremulous, intermitting sound...is productive of the sublime." Such uncertain, wavering, or intermittent sounds leave the listener in fearful anxiety about their cause—like uncertain light or night—and so generate terror and the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ faint, confused, and on-off sounds (or imagery of uncertain light) to cultivate suspense and fearful expectation. The effectiveness depends on surrounding dispositions (e.g., night increases terror). Use intermittent sounds when you wish to exploit uncertainty rather than brute force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cries of animals and inarticulate human voices convey sublime ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Sounds that imitate the natural inarticulate voices of men or animals in pain or danger are capable of conveying great ideas; angry tones of wild beasts likewise produce a great and awful sensation. However, familiar or contemptible creature-voices may fail to awe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting terror or greatness, include cries or animal sounds that signal danger or suffering—universal, non-linguistic vocalizations are readily understood and effective even when the species is unfamiliar. Avoid relying on well-known, contemptible animal sounds that the audience associates with ridicule rather than awe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smell and taste: only extreme bitters and intolerable stenches can produce the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Smells and tastes are weak sources of sublimity, but excessive bitters and intolerable stenches (when moderated in description) can be sources of the sublime because they act as moderated pain. Examples include metaphorical phrases ('A cup of bitterness') and Virgilian images of poisonous exhalations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pungent, bitter, or fetid sensory imagery sparingly and in moderation within descriptive passages to contribute to a sublime atmosphere. Beware of pairing these with mean or contemptible ideas, which degrades the sublime; the test is whether, when united with images of allowed grandeur, the whole composition retains dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling/pain is a central source of the sublime (self-preservation/distress)
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of bodily pain—in labour, anguish, torment—produces the sublime. The sublime belongs to self-preservation; its strongest emotion is distress; no positive pleasure from a direct cause belongs to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy images or narratives of pain, struggle, or distress to elicit the sublime. Recognize that sublime emotion is closely tied to fear and the instincts of self-preservation rather than positive pleasure; many sublime effects rely on this relation to danger and distress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty defined as qualities causing love (distinct from desire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is 'that quality, or those qualities in bodies, by which they cause love, or some passion similar to it.' This definition is confined to merely sensible qualities; the pleasure called 'love' (satisfaction on contemplation) is distinct from desire or lust (which impels possession rather than contemplation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming at beauty in art or description, target the sensible qualities that induce affectionate satisfaction on contemplation rather than arousal of possession or appetite. Distinguish effects that provoke desire (lust) from those that provoke contemplative love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological rules for investigating causes of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Four rules given for inquiry: (1) If two bodies produce the same mental effect and share some properties, attribute the effect to the common properties rather than the differences. (2) Do not explain a natural object's effect by reference to artificial objects. (3) Do not explain a natural object's effect by reasoned conclusions about its uses when a natural cause can be assigned. (4) Do not accept any determinate quantity/relation as the cause of an effect if that effect occurs with different/opposite measures or if the measures can exist without the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these methodological principles when analyzing what causes beauty in an object: prefer common, natural properties as explanations; avoid importing artificial standards; avoid teleological (utility-based) explanations when natural causes are available; and reject fixed numeric proportions as causal when variability contradicts them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion is not the primary cause of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion (relations of measurable quantity) relates chiefly to convenience and the understanding, not to primary sensory causes of beauty. The author argues across vegetables, animals, and humans that beauty appears in widely varying proportions and thus cannot be explained by specific measures; beauty requires no calculative cognition and often exists where strict proportional rules fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on fixed numeric ratios or geometric measures as intrinsic sources of beauty in creative composition. Observe that beautiful effects often persist despite changes in proportion; favour 'manner' (how parts are disposed or presented) over precise measure. Use proportion as a compositional tool if desired, but not as a metaphysical explanation for beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deformity vs beauty and the limited role of custom
rubrics_metrics.description: Deformity opposes the 'complete common form' (anomaly or lack of expected parts) rather than beauty itself. Custom and habitual use tend to deaden our affect: what is habitual often becomes indifferent rather than pleasurable. Beauty strikes often by novelty as much as by conformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish mere absence of deformity from positive beauty; lack of deformity does not guarantee beauty. Beware relying on custom or familiarity to produce beauty—novel or striking arrangements can be essential. When aiming for beauty, consider novelty and manner of presentation rather than merely removing deformities or adhering to customary forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness (utility) is not the cause of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The suitability of parts to their functions (fitness/utility) does not necessarily produce beauty: many admirably 'fit' natural forms (elephant trunk, pelican’s bill, porcupine quills, monkey limbs) are not considered beautiful; usefulness and elegance are distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid equating well-adapted, utilitarian structures with beauty in descriptive practice. Demonstrations of functional efficiency should not be presented as aesthetic praise; instead seek those perceptible sensible qualities that evoke love/pleasure on contemplation. Use functional detail only when it serves an aesthetic purpose, not as a primary justification for calling something beautiful.
